title: EXCLUSIVE: Voting Tech Disaster Risked Forcing Bosnia To Redo Elections In Just Seven Days, Official Said
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
EXCLUSIVE: Voting Tech Disaster Risked Forcing Bosnia To Redo Elections In Just Seven Days, Official Said

‘anull elections and repeat them’

Actual Article Body:
(Francis Kapper / Daily Caller News Foundation)

SARAJEVO, BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA —  Despite issues at polling stations stemming from Bosnia’s nationwide debut of biometric voter checks and ballot scanners, one of the Balkan country’s most politically consequential elections in years successfully concluded.

The ruling political party, the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD), won, potentially paving the way for the creation of a new Christian nation in Europe. Although the election has concluded, the Central Election Commission was considering annulling the results due to major technical difficulties. Here’s what happened under the hood as electoral officials struggled to wrangle the new voting machine technology which ran into major technological hurdles throughout Sunday.

Though the technology was introduced specifically in the Balkan country to combat election irregularities and organized voter manipulation, technical problems emerged almost immediately after polls opened, according to The Associated Press (AP). The election even risked having to be reconducted in a week, a member of the Central Election Commission, Dr. Irena Hadžiabdić, told the Daily Caller News Foundation in an exclusive interview before voting concluded. Hadžiabdić has been a member of the Central Election Commission of Bosnia and Herzegovina since 2007.

The DCNF was on the ground in Banja Luka and Sarajevo documenting the election after spending days covering the political battle leading into the vote. (RELATED: EXCLUSIVE: Here’s How They Host A Trump Rally In The Balkans)

“There are ways to correct serious problems we had at several polling stations, and in that case we always can annul elections and repeat them in seven days,” Hadžiabdić told the DCNF. “But we have to take this decision a little bit later.”

(Francis Kapper / Daily Caller News Foundation)

“I’m, at the moment, in [the nation’s second-largest city,] Banja Luka. My voting place was in Banja Luka, so I’m one of the witnesses. So I was queuing for two hours and [a] half in one of the schools [sic],” Ana Trišić-Babić, who served as Bosnia and Herzegovina’s deputy minister of foreign affairs from 2007 to 2015, told the DCNF before voting concluded. “The scan machines, they were blocking [sic]. Then they were going out as crazy, trying to find technicians, [but] no technicians.”

At the time of writing, it remained unknown if the voting machines will work properly.

“Now we are all waiting,” Hadžiabdić continued. “What will happen after 7 o’clock when we close … most of the polling station[s]? Will these machine[s] work properly and actually be able to transmit all these results that we are waiting for?”

Multiple sources told the DCNF that lines to vote were quickly stretching to last several hours throughout the day. Hadžiabdić spun the issue as proof people are excited to get out and vote.

“I know that sometimes they’re queuing,” Hadžiabdić told the DCNF. “If we always have a queue, if people are interested in elections, I am begging them when I speak publicly during the day to be patient, and we tell them the queuing is sometimes good for democracy. That means that people would like to vote, and we would like to have this increased turnout.”

Multiple polling places could not open voting on time due to problems with the new digital technology, AP reported. Bosnia’s Central Election Commission ultimately said polling stations affected by technical delays would remain open beyond the normal 7 p.m. closing time.

“So it took me literally two hours and [a] half to go,” Trišić-Babić told the DCNF. “Then they were taking out chairs, going out, as you know. It’s not a pleasant situation. Also, to all these people who are running that process, they … didn’t have enough time, probably, to educate, and then they went out at one moment and said, ‘We don’t know what to do. We need to temporarily stop voting.’”
